items.title: What a statistical study does with data
items.core_explanation_md:
A statistical study turns a pile of numbers into a decision in four steps, always in this order:

| Phase | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| Collect | Gather numerical data from the right source |
| Classify and tabulate | Sort the raw data into groups and show it in a table |
| Analyse | Apply formulas and methods that suit the question |
| Interpret | Draw conclusions from the results |

Why bother? Statistics does six jobs: it states facts in definite form, simplifies complicated data, gives a way of comparing, studies how two or more variables move together, supports policy making and helps forecast.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The word "statistics" here means numerical (quantitative) data that can feed further calculation. If a step is skipped, the later ones suffer: analysis done on badly classified data gives a neat-looking but meaningless answer.

self_check.prompt_text: From memory: list the four phases of a statistical study in order, and name three of the six functions of statistics.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Collect, classify and tabulate, analyse, interpret. Functions: present facts definitely, simplify data, compare, study relationships between variables, help in policy making, help in forecasting (any three).

items.title: Statistics in banking, and where it stops
items.core_explanation_md:
Banks lean on statistics because their decisions rest on large numbers of accounts and transactions. Credit policy, for example, is set after studying profitability, demand and time deposits, credit ratios and customer numbers, and the policy itself rests on probability theory.

Four limits keep this honest:

- **Aggregates, not individuals.** Statistics describes groups; it says little about one particular borrower.
- **Numbers only.** Purely qualitative facts must first be turned into numbers before statistics can handle them.
- **Averages, not certainties.** Results are true on average over the long run, because a sample stands in for the whole.
- **Bias in, bias out.** Careless or dishonest data collection ruins the whole investigation.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A useful habit: before trusting a statistical claim, ask who collected the data and how. The first three limits are built into the method; the fourth is a failure of people.

self_check.prompt_text: A manager says "statistics proves that this borrower will default". Which limitation of statistics does that statement ignore?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Statistics deals with aggregates and long-run averages, not with individual cases; it can say how likely default is across a group, not what one borrower will do.

items.title: Population and sample, parameter and statistic
items.core_explanation_md:
Two pairs of words carry most of this unit.

| Group-wide | Part-wide |
| --- | --- |
| **Population**: every observation you want to draw conclusions about | **Sample**: a part of the population actually studied |
| **Parameter**: a number describing the population (fixed, usually unknown) | **Statistic**: a number computed from the sample, used to estimate the parameter |

Example in a bank: the population is the balances of all savings accounts in a region. Average balance of all of them is a parameter. If you look at 400 accounts and compute their average, that average is a statistic, and you use it to estimate the unknown parameter.
items.expanded_explanation_md: We sample because the population is often too large, too costly or too slow to study in full. The sample must be representative, otherwise the statistic will mislead about the parameter. A statistic is also called an estimator.

self_check.prompt_text: You compute the average loan size of 250 randomly picked accounts out of 40,000. Is the result a parameter or a statistic, and what does it estimate?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It is a statistic. It estimates the parameter: the average loan size of all 40,000 accounts.

items.title: Attributes, variates, discrete and continuous
items.core_explanation_md:
Ask one question of any characteristic: *can it be written as a number?*

- No: it is an **attribute** (type of account, branch location, religion, colour).
- Yes: it is a **variate** (balance, age, number of dependants). A variate is then split by the values it can take:

| Kind of variate | Takes | Banking examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Discrete | Separate, countable values | Number of loan accounts a customer holds; cheques returned in a month |
| Continuous | Any value in a range, whole or fractional | Account balance in rupees and paise; time taken to process a loan |

Counting gives discrete data; measuring gives continuous data.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Watch out for rounded measurements. Age is continuous in principle, even though it is often reported in whole years; the courseware lists "age in years" as discrete, so read the question for how the variable is being recorded.

self_check.prompt_text: Classify each: (a) type of deposit scheme, (b) number of ATMs in a district, (c) time a customer waits at the counter.
self_check.expected_takeaway: (a) attribute, (b) discrete variate, (c) continuous variate.

items.title: Primary or secondary data, census or survey
items.core_explanation_md:
Data comes from one of two places, and is collected on one of two scales.

| | Primary data | Secondary data |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Collected | First time, directly from respondents | Earlier, by someone else, for another purpose |
| Usual methods or sources | Direct interview, questionnaires | Records, published reports, banks, research bodies, the internet |
| Cost in money, time, effort | Higher | Lower |
| Fit to your question | Designed for it | Must be checked |

The same figures can be primary for one user and secondary for another: a statistical table is primary for the office that gathered it and secondary for the analyst who reuses it.

On scale: a **census** covers every unit of the population, while a **sample survey** covers a part and generalises to the whole, which works only if the sample is representative.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Choosing is a trade-off. If a good secondary source already answers the question, using it saves money and time. If it does not fit, primary collection is worth its cost.

self_check.prompt_text: A bank wants customer opinion on a new app feature. Would you start with primary or secondary data, and why?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Primary data (for example a questionnaire), because existing records will not hold opinions on a feature the customers have only just seen.

items.title: Classifying data: four bases and how many ways
items.core_explanation_md:
Classification sorts raw data into groups that share a characteristic. It shrinks a long list into a few classes you can compare, and it is the step before tabulation.

**Base** (what you sort by):

| Base | Sorted by | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Qualitative | A quality or attribute | Deposit accounts by type of scheme |
| Quantitative | A numerical characteristic | Borrowers by loan amount |
| Geographical | Place | Deposits by state |
| Chronological | Time of occurrence | Quarter-wise gross NPAs (a time series) |

**Number of ways** (how many characteristics at once): one characteristic is *one-way*, two is *two-way* and more than two is *multi-way*.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A table with branch type down the side and account type across the top is a two-way classification. Adding a third characteristic, such as year, makes it multi-way.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the base and the number of ways: customers classified by city and by gender.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Geographical and qualitative bases, classified two-way.

items.title: Class width, class mark and class boundaries
items.core_explanation_md:
Each class in a frequency table has a lower limit and an upper limit. Two quantities describe it:

- the **width** says how big the class is;
- the **class mark** is the middle of the class, used to stand for every value in it.

In an **exclusive** series (0-10, 10-20, ...) a value equal to the upper limit is counted in the next class. In an **inclusive** series (60-69, 70-79, ...) both limits belong to the class. To get continuous classes from an inclusive series, widen each class by half the gap between one upper limit and the next lower limit: these are the **class boundaries**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: If you are asked for a class width when only the data are given, divide the range (largest minus smallest value) by the number of classes wanted. Boundaries are what make inclusive classes safe to use in calculations that treat the variable as continuous.

formula_spec.latex_expression: \text{width} = U - L,\quad m = \frac{L + U}{2},\quad L_b = L - \frac{g}{2},\quad U_b = U + \frac{g}{2}

variables.name: Gap between the upper limit of one inclusive class and the lower limit of the next

assumptions: For width and mark, use the limits of the class as given (exclusive) or its boundaries (inclusive); both give the same width and mark for equal-width inclusive classes.
Classes of equal width cover the observed range without a break.
common_errors: Using 1 instead of half the gap when widening inclusive limits (the adjustment is half of the gap, so 0.5 for a gap of 1).
Counting a value equal to an upper limit in the lower class of an exclusive series.
Subtracting limits of an inclusive class to get the width (9 - 5 = 4) instead of using boundaries (9.5 - 4.5 = 5).

self_check.prompt_text: Inclusive classes run 1-5, 6-10, 11-15. Give the boundaries of the middle class and its mark.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Gap is 1, so adjust by 0.5: boundaries 5.5 to 10.5; mark (6 + 10)/2 = 8.

items.title: Relative, percentage frequency and frequency density
items.core_explanation_md:
Raw class frequencies are hard to compare across tables of different sizes, so express each as a share of the total:

- **Relative frequency** is a fraction of 1;
- **Percentage frequency** is the same share out of 100.

When classes have unequal widths, a bigger class naturally collects more observations. **Frequency density** removes that effect by dividing by width, so you can see where observations really crowd together.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Relative frequencies of all classes add to 1 (or to 100 for percentages), which is a handy check on your arithmetic. Density only matters when widths differ; with equal widths it just rescales the frequencies.

variables.name: Relative frequency, percentage frequency, frequency density
variables.unit: fraction, per cent, observations per unit of the variable

assumptions: N is the sum of all class frequencies in the table.
Width is measured in the same unit for every class.
common_errors: Dividing by the number of classes instead of the total frequency.
Forgetting the factor 100 for the percentage frequency.
Comparing raw frequencies of classes of different widths instead of their densities.

self_check.prompt_text: A class holds 18 of 75 observations. What are its relative and percentage frequencies?

items.title: Cumulative frequencies: less-than and more-than
items.core_explanation_md:
A cumulative frequency answers "how many observations are at or below this point?" or "at or above?" without adding up the table each time.

| Type | How it is built | What the last or first entry shows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Less-than | Add class frequencies from the lowest class upwards | The final entry equals the total |
| More-than (greater-than) | Add them from the highest class downwards | The first entry equals the total |

The two always pair up: the less-than count at a boundary plus the more-than count at the same boundary give the total.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Each cumulative value is tied to a class boundary, not to a class. "Less than 30" means everything below the boundary 30.

self_check.prompt_text: Classes 0-10, 10-20, 20-30 have frequencies 5, 9, 6. Write the less-than cumulative frequencies.
self_check.expected_takeaway: 5, 14 and 20 (cumulative counts below 10, 20 and 30).

items.title: Why banks sample, and the symbols that go with it
items.core_explanation_md:
Studying every item is rarely possible: the population may be huge, testing may destroy the item, and time and money are limited. So you take a **sample**, measure it, and generalise to the **population**. A full count (a **census**) is the exception.

Keep the notation straight; the letter tells you which world a number belongs to:

| | Population | Sample |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Size | N | n |
| Mean | mu | x-bar |
| Standard deviation | sigma | s |
| Name of such a number | parameter | statistic |

Sampling is only as good as the sample: if it is not representative, every conclusion drawn from it is shaky.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Why this matters in a bank: a credit-quality review of 20 lakh loan accounts cannot read every file. A sample read carefully tells more than a census read carelessly, provided the sample is well chosen.

self_check.prompt_text: From memory: which letters stand for population size, sample size, population mean and sample mean?
self_check.expected_takeaway: N, n, mu and x-bar respectively.

items.title: Judgement samples, random samples and bias
items.core_explanation_md:
There are two ways to choose a sample.

| | Judgement (non-random) | Random (probability) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who picks | Someone's knowledge or opinion | Chance, with known probabilities |
| Strength | Quick, convenient, good for a pilot | Every item has a chance of selection |
| Weakness | Its validity cannot be tested; rigorous statistical analysis is not possible | Needs a list of the population and more effort |

**Bias** creeps in when you pick the people most likely to have strong views, for example surveying only those directly affected by a policy. The report then describes that group, not the public. Random selection avoids this, and it allows the reliability of the estimate to be worked out.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A judgement sample is not worthless: a branch manager choosing three typical branches to pilot a new form is sensible. The mistake is treating the pilot result as if it were a scientifically drawn sample.

self_check.prompt_text: Why can the reliability of an estimate be worked out for a random sample but not for a judgement sample?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Random selection gives known chances of inclusion, so statistical theory applies; a judgement sample depends on the chooser's opinion, so its representativeness cannot be tested.

items.title: Simple random sampling: equal chances, with or without replacement
items.core_explanation_md:
In **simple random sampling** every possible sample has the same chance of being picked, and so does every member of the population.

Small example: from four officers A, B, C, D choose two. There are six possible pairs (AB, AC, AD, BC, BD, CD), each with probability 1/6, and each officer is in three of the six, so each has a 1/2 chance of being chosen.

Two ways to draw:

- **Without replacement**: a chosen item is set aside, so it cannot appear twice.
- **With replacement**: the item is put back before the next draw, so it can be chosen again.

For big populations, slips in a box do not work. Give each member a number and read numbers from a computer or a table of random digits, where every digit from 0 to 9 is equally likely.
items.expanded_explanation_md: An "infinite" population in statistics does not mean literally infinite. It means one too large to list in reasonable time, treated as if it never runs out.

self_check.prompt_text: Five officers, sample of two without replacement. How many possible samples are there, and what is the chance that a particular officer is in the sample?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Ten possible samples; each officer is in four of them, so the chance is 4/10 = 2/5.

items.title: Stratified or cluster sampling: which one, and why
items.core_explanation_md:
Both start by dividing the population into groups. They differ in what the groups look like, and so in what you do next.

| | Stratified | Cluster |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Groups | **Strata**: similar inside, different from each other | **Clusters**: much alike each other, varied inside |
| What you sample | Items at random from **every** stratum | A random few clusters, then **every** item in them |
| How many from each | In proportion to stratum size, or equal numbers weighted afterwards | Whole clusters |
| Use when | The population is already in groups of different sizes | The groups look like small copies of the whole, and cost matters |

A quick test: *is there little variation within groups and a lot between them?* Use stratified. *Is it the other way round?* Use cluster.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Stratifying a bank's customers into retail, small business and corporate makes sense because they behave very differently. Treating each branch as a cluster of a mixed customer base, and surveying all customers in a few branches, is cheaper and works if branches resemble one another.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Stratified sampling, with the number drawn from each segment proportional to its share of customers (or equal numbers, weighted later by share).

items.title: Sampling distributions and standard error
items.core_explanation_md:
Take one sample and you get one mean. Take another sample of the same size and you get a different mean. If you could take **every** possible sample of that size, the collection of all their means is the **sampling distribution of the mean**. The same idea gives a sampling distribution for a median or a proportion.

Two facts to carry away:

- the sample means cluster around the population mean (their average equals it), and they are less spread out than the individual values;
- the standard deviation of that distribution is the **standard error**. It measures how far a sample mean is likely to stray from the truth by chance alone.

Smaller standard error means a better, more reliable estimator.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Do not confuse the two spreads. The standard deviation describes how individual items vary. The standard error describes how the sample *means* vary. The second is always smaller for n greater than 1.

self_check.prompt_text: What does the standard error of the mean measure, in one sentence?
self_check.expected_takeaway: How much sample means vary from sample to sample, because of chance, around the population mean.

items.title: Standard error of the mean and the z value of a sample mean
items.core_explanation_md:
For samples of size n from a population with mean mu and standard deviation sigma (infinite population, or sampling with replacement), the sampling distribution of the mean has the same centre as the population and a smaller spread:

- centre: mu of x-bar equals mu;
- spread: the standard error is sigma divided by the square root of n.

To find how likely a sample mean is to fall beyond a given value, measure the distance in standard errors and use the standard normal table: z is the sample mean minus mu, divided by the standard error. Areas on opposite sides of zero are added, on the same side subtracted.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The z value is unit-free, so the same table serves rupees, days or percentages. If the population is normal, this works for any n. If it is not, use it when n is at least 30 (central limit theorem).

items.title: The central limit theorem in practice
items.core_explanation_md:
Real populations are rarely bell-shaped: loan sizes, deposit balances and claim amounts are usually skewed. The **central limit theorem** rescues us:

- whatever the shape of the population, the mean of the sampling distribution equals the population mean;
- as the sample size grows, the **shape** of the sampling distribution of the mean approaches the normal curve.

In practice you do not need an enormous sample. Use the normal approximation when **n is at least 30**; for fairly well-behaved populations even about 15 may be enough. The payoff: you can make probability statements about a sample mean without knowing the shape of the population.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The theorem is about sample means (and sums), not about individual values. A skewed population stays skewed; it is the distribution of the averages that becomes bell-shaped.

self_check.prompt_text: A population of account balances is heavily skewed. Can you use the normal table for the mean of a random sample of 50 accounts? Why?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Yes. With n of at least 30 the central limit theorem makes the sampling distribution of the mean approximately normal, whatever the population shape.

items.title: Finite population multiplier and the 5 per cent rule
items.core_explanation_md:
Sampling **without replacement** from a **finite** population gives more information per item than the plain formula credits, because each item drawn leaves fewer unknowns. The standard error is multiplied by a correction, the **finite population multiplier**, which is below 1.

The **sampling fraction** n/N tells you whether it matters. If the sample is a tiny share of the population, the multiplier is almost 1 and can be dropped. The accepted rule: when n/N is **less than 0.05**, skip the multiplier.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Notice what precision depends on. With the multiplier dropped, the standard error depends only on n, the absolute size of the sample, not on how big a slice of the population it is. A sample of 400 from a very large population is as precise as 400 from a larger one.

assumptions: Population finite and sampling without replacement.
The multiplier may be omitted when n/N is less than 0.05.
common_errors: Applying the multiplier when sampling with replacement.
Using N - n over N instead of N - n over N - 1.
Forgetting that the multiplier is inside a square root.

self_check.prompt_text: N = 65 and n = 16. Is the sampling fraction large enough that the multiplier matters, and what is the multiplier?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Sampling fraction 16/65, about 0.25, is above 0.05, so it matters. Multiplier = square root of 49/64 = 7/8 = 0.875.

items.title: More sample, less error: diminishing returns
items.core_explanation_md:
Because the standard error is sigma over the square root of n, it falls as the sample grows, but ever more slowly:

| Sample size | Standard error when sigma = 100 |
| --- | --- |
| 10 | 31.63 |
| 100 | 10 |

A tenfold bigger sample cuts the error to roughly one-third, not one-tenth. To halve the error you must **quadruple** the sample.

So the right sample size is a decision, not a maximum: compare the value of the extra precision with the cost of collecting the extra observations.
items.expanded_explanation_md: This is the law of diminishing returns borrowed from economics. A common reasoning error is to think that sampling "half as many" accounts gives half the accuracy. It costs you far less than that, which is why modest samples are used so often.

self_check.prompt_text: If you want the standard error to drop to one-third of its present value, by what factor must the sample size rise?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Nine times, because the standard error varies as 1 divided by the square root of n.

items.stem_md: A bank assesses customer satisfaction by interviewing only customers who came to the complaints desk during one week. The result is most likely

options.text_md: Unbiased, because the number of customers interviewed was large
options.explanation_md: A large number of respondents does not repair a flawed selection.

options.text_md: Unbiased, because every customer is a bank customer

options.text_md: Biased, because it chooses people likely to have strong negative feelings
options.explanation_md: Selecting those with strong feelings gives a biased sample that does not reflect the overall customer base.

options.text_md: Systematic, because it covers one fixed week
options.explanation_md: Systematic sampling means a fixed interval from a random start; this is a convenience selection.

items.correct_explanation_md: Choosing people who are likely to hold strong views produces a biased sample, so the result will not reflect all customers.

items.stem_md: Daily ATM withdrawal data are sampled by taking every seventh day. Why could this give a misleading average?

options.text_md: Because systematic sampling gives items unequal chances of selection
options.explanation_md: Each day has an equal chance; the problem is the pattern.

options.text_md: Because a seven-day interval can match a weekly cycle in withdrawals and pick the same weekday each time
options.explanation_md: When the interval coincides with a pattern in the population, the sample is biased.

options.text_md: Because the sample size is always too small
options.explanation_md: The size is not the issue.

options.text_md: Because replacement is not allowed
options.explanation_md: Replacement has nothing to do with the interval problem.

items.correct_explanation_md: The risk in systematic sampling is that the interval matches a periodic pattern in the data. A weekly interval on a weekly cycle always lands on the same weekday.

items.stem_md: A bank groups its branches by region. Within each region, branches are very similar, but regions differ a lot. The bank wants a sample of branches. Which method suits this population best?

options.text_md: Cluster sampling, because the groups differ from each other
options.explanation_md: Cluster sampling suits groups that are alike each other with wide variation inside.

options.text_md: Judgement sampling, because regions differ
options.explanation_md: Judgement sampling cannot be tested for representativeness.

options.text_md: Stratified sampling, drawing branches from every region
options.explanation_md: Little variation within groups and wide variation between them calls for stratified sampling.

options.text_md: Systematic sampling, because regions repeat
options.explanation_md: Nothing in the description suggests a regular interval.

items.correct_explanation_md: Stratified sampling is used when groups are homogeneous inside and differ between themselves; the sample is taken from every group.

items.stem_md: A bank wants to survey customers cheaply. Each branch has a similar mix of customers, with wide variety inside, and branches look alike. The best plan is

options.text_md: Choose a few branches at random and survey all customers in them
options.explanation_md: Groups that are alike each other but varied inside are suited to cluster sampling.

options.text_md: Choose some customers from every branch in proportion to branch size
options.explanation_md: This is stratified sampling, which pays off when groups differ from each other.

options.text_md: Survey every tenth customer who happens to walk in
options.explanation_md: This is convenience selection, not a probability design.

options.text_md: Choose the branch the regional head thinks is typical
options.explanation_md: This is a judgement sample.

items.correct_explanation_md: When groups are alike each other but each is internally varied, a random selection of clusters, with every unit in them examined, is precise and cheaper.

items.stem_md: The standard error of the mean is best described as

options.text_md: The standard deviation of individual values in the population
options.explanation_md: That is the population standard deviation, sigma.

options.text_md: The standard deviation of the distribution of sample means
options.explanation_md: It measures how far sample means vary around the population mean through chance.

options.text_md: The mistake made by a careless interviewer
options.explanation_md: It refers to chance variation in sampling, not blunders.

options.text_md: The sample mean minus the population mean in one particular sample
options.explanation_md: That is the sampling error in a single sample, not the standard deviation of all of them.

items.correct_explanation_md: The standard error of the mean is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the mean.

items.stem_md: Loan sizes are strongly skewed. A random sample of 64 loans is drawn repeatedly, and the sample mean is computed each time. The distribution of these sample means will be

options.text_md: Skewed in the same way as the loan sizes
options.explanation_md: The shape of the means changes with n; it does not copy the population.

options.text_md: Approximately normal, with mean equal to the population mean
options.explanation_md: By the central limit theorem, with n of at least 30 the sampling distribution of the mean is approximately normal.

options.text_md: Approximately normal, but centred below the population mean
options.explanation_md: The mean of the sampling distribution equals the population mean.

options.text_md: Impossible to describe without knowing the population shape
options.explanation_md: The theorem exists to avoid exactly that requirement.

items.correct_explanation_md: The central limit theorem says the sampling distribution of the mean approaches the normal distribution as n grows, whatever the population shape, and its mean is the population mean.

options.text_md: Fall to one-quarter of its value
options.explanation_md: It varies with the square root of n, not with n.

options.text_md: Fall to one-half of its value
options.explanation_md: The square root of 4 is 2, so the standard error is divided by 2.

options.text_md: Remain unchanged
options.explanation_md: The standard error depends on n.

options.text_md: Double
options.explanation_md: A larger sample reduces the standard error.

items.correct_explanation_md: The standard error is sigma divided by the square root of n. Multiplying n by 4 divides the standard error by 2.
